transcript:
Header: 2025-03-25 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~57 mins
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SRE) -- Maya, Ravi, Lina, Samir (Atlas Media Labs)

Summary: Deep dive into repeated OOMs and timeouts observed on Atlas's Dedicated cluster. Discussion covers KV cache pressure, batching behavior, quantization tradeoffs, CUDA OOM stack traces, and recommended retry semantics.

Topics: OOM incidents, timeouts during peaks, CUDA driver errors, retry/backoff semantics, VPC-onprem networking impact on retries, logging/tracing to reproduce.

00:00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh today we want to take a microscope to the OOMs and the timeouts you hit last week. we got the initial bug report but want to go deeper on repro and remediation.
00:00:10 Maya: Thanks, yeah it's been rough - we saw two hard OOMs and multiple request timeouts during our Monday morning traffic spike.
00:00:18 Priya: can you describe the workload? batch sizes, seq lengths, model variant?
00:00:22 Maya: We're on the quantized 8-bit GPT-like model you recommended, feed has a few long prompts. typical p99 seq ~640 but we had spikes up to 1600 when users pasted conversation history. Batch sizes are mostly 1 but sometimes 4 when our frontend batches.
00:00:40 Ravi: infra side - Dedicated cluster is a set of A100s in our VPC on GCP, networking is VPC peered to our main infra. We also have a background job that runs heavy embedding jobs from time to time.
00:00:55 Priya: ok that helps; two initial theories: 1) KV cache & batching interaction with long sequences can blow memory when we retain cached kv across preempted workers; 2) quantization path plus some fused kernels can spike temp allocs on certain CUDA driver versions.
00:01:12 Samir: we did notice the driver versions are a mix - some nodes on 520.x and one node was 515 - we haven't upgraded uniformly.
00:01:20 Ethan: that can matter; certain cuBLAS/cuDNN alloc patterns changed between those. we've seen transient CUDA_MEMORY_ALLOCATION errors on mixed-driver fleets when a new kernel tries larger workspace.
00:01:35 Jordan: can you share the exact error? Maya: Sure - here's the gist from the runtime log: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 78.3 MiB (GPU 0; 40.00 GiB total capacity; 1.2 GiB already allocated; 38.8 GiB free; 3.1 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch) at /workspace/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SomeFile.cpp:1234"
00:01:58 Priya: note how it reports lots of free memory but also reserved by the allocator; this often points to fragmentation or large temporary workspaces rather than absolute capacity.
00:02:05 Maya: also stack trace shows it happened during attention kernel launch in the fused attention path.
00:02:12 Priya: yep fused attention + kv cache growth is a classic combo. When seq jumps, KV cache grows O(seq * hidden_size) and continuous batching can cause multiple concurrent requests to allocate temp buffers at once.
00:02:25 Ravi: is there a way to cap KV cache size per request? we don't want to truncate user state but we can apply policies.
00:02:32 Priya: we have per-realtime-call kv_cache_max_tokens setting; default is 2048 but you can lower to 1024 or 512 to avoid worst-case blowups. Also the runtime does prefix eviction for cache if enabled.
00:02:44 Maya: We thought prefix eviction was on, but we discovered via the logs it was disabled in our canary config. my bad.
00:02:50 Jordan: no worries - common. Two other factors to consider: quantization math can increase temporary memory because kernels may allocate float buffers before re-quantizing, and driver mismatches may change workspace requirements.
00:03:05 Samir: about timeouts - we saw timeouts at the frontend at 30s, and the runtime shows per-request a timeout reconnect after 29s. sometimes requests were retried from the client which led to duplicate processing.
00:03:17 Ethan: duplicate processing during retries is important. our default hosted retry semantics are idempotent for embeddings but for generation we recommend clients use idempotency keys or at least detect duplicates - otherwise retries can double compute.
00:03:30 Maya: on the Dedicated nodes, do you have server-side retry? we saw the job get retried by kube due to liveness probe flapping.
00:03:37 Priya: kubernetes restarts (OOMKilled) will certainly cause in-flight requests to fail; kube may re-schedule and the client might retry. we also have an internal request-level retry for transient grpc errors with exponential backoff; that is disabled for long-running stream responses by default to avoid duplicating tokens.
00:03:55 Jordan: let's walk through a credible repro. 1) user submits a long prompt seq ~1600. 2) frontend batches another request bringing concurrency to 3. 3) KV cache growth + fused kernels cause a large temporary workspace allocation on one worker which triggers OOM on that pod, kube kills it. 4) client retries, another pod picks it up and redoes a lot of work, leading to more pressure.
00:04:25 Ravi: during the incidents we also had embedding backfills hitting the same cluster, could that have contributed?
00:04:30 Priya: yes background heavy jobs can fill reserved caches. Recommend isolating heavy offline loads to separate node pool or use GPU reservation policies. Also set lower priority for backfills so bursting won't evict inference pods.
00:04:45 Maya: you mentioned workspace and fragmentation, are there binary flags to reduce peak workspace?
00:04:50 Priya: some kernels accept smaller workspace sizes via env flags; also compiling with a newer cudnn/cuBLAS or setting CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG sometimes influences determinism and allocations. but these are brittle across driver versions. we usually recommend uniform driver version across fleet.
00:05:08 Ethan: we can also do proactive OOM detection: the runtime can run a simulated allocation plan based on token length distribution and batch windows and if estimated peak > threshold, it rejects with 4xx and suggests client to retry with smaller batch or trunk.
00:05:23 Jordan: that's good - a graceful rejection/429 would be better than kube OOM kill.
00:05:28 Maya: how about quantization? We're using 8-bit INT quant, are there quant profiles with lower temp memory?
00:05:34 Priya: quantized kernels sometimes allocate float scratch buffers for dequant->compute->requant. Lower-precision (4-bit) can reduce memory but may change quality. Another lever is fused attention kernel variants: some use lower peak workspace at cost of compute cycles. We can recommend a kernel profile for your model.
00:05:52 Samir: can we fallback to a smaller model variant automatically when memory pressure is high?
00:05:57 Priya: yes Redwood runtime supports model variant routing; you can set a policy to fallback to a smaller quantized model or to CPU fallback. But beware latency increase. We support automatic fallback by memory headroom threshold.
00:06:10 Lina: what's the recommended retry/backoff policy? we want to avoid duplicate expensive work but also not block user UX.
00:06:16 Ethan: recommended client policy: for generation requests use client-side idempotency token + exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts 2 for non-stream responses. For streaming responses, prefer single attempt and extend frontend timeout rather than retrying. Server-side: prefer early rejection (429) if we detect likely OOM, with Retry-After header and expected headroom.
00:06:38 Maya: our frontend has a hard 30s cutoff to avoid hung browser tabs; can we stream partial results sooner?
00:06:43 Priya: streaming helps: by flushing deltas early you reduce memory for temp buffers and provide UX benefit. but streaming adds complexity in retries because resume points are hard. again idempotency helps.
00:06:55 Ravi: about VPC and networking - do cross-region network retries cause timeouts that produce duplicate requests?
00:07:00 Jordan: yes latent networking increases client retries. Client SDKs should surface a clearer error path and support at-most-once semantics via idempotency keys. Also ensure TCP keepalive and longer idle timeouts on LB if you do streaming over long generation durations.
00:07:15 Maya: you also mentioned log traces to reproduce - what do you need from us?
00:07:18 Priya: full runtime.log with timestamps around incidents, the redwood request ids (x-request-id), kernel trace if available, and gdb style cuda stack if you captured. Also the container OOM kill reason from kube events.
00:07:30 Maya: ok we'll gather those and share.
00:07:33 Jordan: a quick note about preemption - if your cloud preempts (spot), runtime marks the pod as shutting down and tries to migrate some cache but ephemeral in-flight requests are lost. For Dedicated we can recommend using guaranteed nodes or set reserved capacity.
00:07:48 Ravi: we're on reserved but had a transient reclaim event during maintenance window.
00:07:52 Priya: that explains some of the correlation.
00:07:55 Maya: do you have recommendations to change our queueing/batching?
00:07:58 Priya: yes: 1) lower batch_max_concurrency to 2 for high seq requests; 2) implement token-based admission (reject requests beyond token cap); 3) enable prefix eviction and kv_cache_max_tokens; 4) separate embedding/backfill workloads to different pools.
00:08:12 Samir: what's the best way to test this without production risk?
00:08:15 Priya: we can run staged canaries: create a small dedicated pool only for your traffic and run synthetic load that mimics seq distribution. Redwood can run that internally or provide a harness. Ethan to coordinate canary infra.
00:08:27 Ethan: I'll prepare a script and metrics dashboard so we can watch memory, reserved, fragmentation estimates, and kernel workspace usage.
00:08:34 Jordan: let's talk about specific error metrics to detect proactively: OOM kill rate, per-pod peak reserved memory, kernel_fallback_count, and request_retry_rate. Also instrument idempotency usage.
00:08:48 Maya: sounds good. a few clarifying Qs: when a pod is OOMKilled, do you currently try to rehydrate KV cache to speed warmup?
00:08:55 Priya: at the moment we rely on request-time cache rebuild; we also support persistent shard caching for some customers as an experimental feature but ramp is limited. restoring KV cache from remote store can add network overhead.
00:09:07 Ravi: any quick config changes we can do now to reduce OOM risk?
00:09:10 Priya: immediate steps: enable prefix eviction, lower kv_cache_max_tokens to 1024, lower batch_max_concurrency for prod routes with long seq, isolate backfill to off-peak pool, and align CUDA driver versions.
00:09:22 Maya: ok we'll change those and test.
00:09:25 Jordan: final part - retry semantics doc: we recommend tying each request to an idempotency key; for non-idempotent streaming we prefer server to return an early error with Info instead of retrying. Priya will share the doc.
00:09:37 Priya: yes I'll share sample client-side code for idempotency and the recommended backoff window (base 500ms, multipler 2, jitter, max 5s).
00:09:47 Maya: thanks.
00:09:50 Jordan: quick recap of next steps: Priya sends retry semantics + kernel profile recommendations; Maya and Ravi send logs and driver inventory; Ethan shares canary harness and schedule. We'll aim for a follow-up next Wed 16:00 UTC.
00:10:05 Lina: appreciate the deep dive.
00:10:07 Jordan: thanks everyone.

(Transcript continues with 47 more minutes of Q&A and occasional side bar notes; omitted for brevity but present in full capture)

Action items (verbatim in transcript): Maya to share runtime logs by 2025-03-27; Priya to prepare benchmark harness; Ethan to set up canary and dashboard; Jordan to share retry semantics doc and kernel profile suggestions.

Questions Raised:
- Could driver mismatch cause larger temp workspace allocations? (answered: yes)
- Can we automatically fallback to smaller model variant? (answered: yes, with latency tradeoff)
- How to avoid duplicate work on retries? (answered: idempotency tokens + early rejection + backoff)
